newsitem.title: USA: Former defense chiefs attack chemical weapons pact.
newsitem.headline: Former defense chiefs attack chemical weapons pact.

text.p: Four Republican former defence secretaries criticised an international treaty outlawing chemical weapons on Tuesday, asserting it would be ignored by "rogue" states and could not prevent cheating.

Opponents and supporters of the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention crossed swords at a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing chaired by Sen. Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican and leading foe of the pact.
"The case against this treaty can be summarized quite simply: it is not global, it is not verifiable, it is not constitutional, and it will not work," Helms said at the start of the hearing.

Former defence secretaries James Schlesinger, Caspar Weinberger and Donald Rumsfeld appeared before the committee and Dick Cheney, defence secretary under President George Bush, argued against the treaty in a letter to Helms.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was appearing later on Tuesday to make the Clinton administration's case for Senate approval of the treaty.

As the senators heard arguments on the treaty, Clinton told reporters at the White House: "If we don't ratify it then the rest of the world will be compelled to treat us like rogue states, to basically ostracize us and impose trade sanctions on our chemical companies. And we'll deserve it if we don't ratify it because we won't be good citizens in the world."

The 1993 treaty bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons. It comes into force on April 29 and officials say that unless the Senate approves it before then the United States will have no say in its implementation.
Both sides in the debate have recruited long lists of critics or endorsers of the treaty from among former high officials and military officers.

Helms, flanked by two leading Senate supporters of the treaty, Democrat Joseph Biden of Delaware and Republican Richard Lugar of Indiana, said the pact "is much worse than nothing." He said it would increase "rogue" regimes' access to chemical agents and impose new regulations on U.S. businesses, exposing them to increased danger of industrial espionage and trampling on their constitutional rights.

"Outside the (Washington) beltway, where people don't worship at the altar of arms control, that's what we call a bum deal," Helms said. He said negotiations with Biden on concerns about the treaty had reached agreement on about 21 "relatively minor defects" but the administration was "stonewalling" on five or six major issues.
Weinberger told the committee it was "absurd" to rush to a vote, saying it was worth waiting to craft U.S. reservations to a "well-intentioned but badly flawed" treaty.
Rumsfeld said ratification would cause people to believe erroneously that the threat of chemical weapons had been dealt with, leading to complacency.

He said smaller U.S. chemical firms would suffer a risk to proprietary information while large companies would have the resources to avoid such problems. The pact is strongly backed by the Chemical Manufacturers Association.
Schlesinger said Iraq's use of poison gas had shown that treaties could do little to prevent its use or manufacture.
But Biden said the treaty would open the way to international pressure against countries with illegal chemical weapons programmes, asserting, "Norms do matter."

The Foreign Relations Committee approved the treaty on a 13-5 vote a year ago, but it was withdrawn from the full Senate in September at the administration's request after Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole opposed it, endangering prospects of getting a needed two-thirds majority.
To return to the full Senate the treaty must again get a positive committee vote.
